The initial wet weight of the egg, calculated from its dimensions of 30 millimeters in length and 20 millimeters in width, yields a mass of approximately 6.3 grams [Ww0 = approximately 6.3 grams], a substantial investment that represents roughly 14 percent of the adult female's body mass and underscores the high per-offspring energetic commitment characteristic of caprimulgids. Embryonic development proceeds over a period of 20 days [ab = 20 days] when the incubating parent maintains the egg at a temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], a thermal regime that reflects the cooler microclimate of its montane Andean habitat. Field records indicate that this incubation duration aligns closely with that documented in the congener Uropsalis lyra, suggesting a conserved developmental schedule within the genus. The altricial hatchling emerges weighing less than a seventh of the adult female, relying entirely on parental provisioning during the early nestling phase.

Under the consistently elevated body temperatures characteristic of active adult nightjars, measured at approximately 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], the nestling period proceeds through a precisely timed developmental sequence. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest site, occurs 20 days after hatching [tx = 20 days after hatching], a relatively short nestling phase that likely reduces predation risk in exposed montane nesting locations at a temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C]. This timing is comparable to that reported for the related species Uropsalis lyra, suggesting a phylogenetic constraint on developmental rate. Gonadal maturation and the attainment of puberty follow considerably later, with individuals reaching sexual maturity at 63 days after hatching [tp = 63 days after hatching] when maintained under the same thermal conditions at a temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C]. This 63-day interval between hatching and reproductive competence reflects the extended period required for full somatic growth and the development of the elongated outer rectrices that characterize adult plumage.

Reproductive output in the Swallow-tailed nightjar is constrained by a single-egg clutch and a strict annual breeding schedule. Females typically lay one egg per clutch [N_R_i = one egg per clutch], and field observations confirm that they produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = a single clutch each year], a remarkably conservative reproductive strategy even by nightjar standards. This slow pace of reproduction, set against the backdrop of a typical adult body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], suggests that each reproductive attempt represents a substantial energetic investment for the female. The solitary egg is relatively large at 6.3 grams [Ww0 = 6.3 grams], representing over fourteen percent of the female's body mass, which may constrain the frequency with which breeding can occur. The extended incubation and brooding duties are shared between the sexes, a biparental care pattern that facilitates the successful rearing of the single offspring.

This interval between hatching and the initiation of first reproduction reflects the time needed to complete somatic growth, acquire a territory, and secure a mate in the competitive montane environment. Maximal longevity, based on the oldest documented individuals, reaches 3358 days since birth [am = 3358 days since birth] when measured at the same body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], a lifespan that spans nearly ten years. Such longevity is notable for a bird of this body mass and may be linked to the low annual mortality rates afforded by a conservative, single-offspring reproductive strategy. Individuals that successfully navigate the early survival bottlenecks can therefore enjoy a long reproductive window.

Basal metabolic rate in Uropsalis segmentata, measured during the inactive phase at a body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], is approximately 98.18 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = approximately 98.18 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a rate consistent with the moderate metabolic demands of a 40-gram caprimulgid. This measurement, obtained from respirometry trials on post-absorptive adults at rest, places the species within the expected range for nightjars, which generally exhibit slightly reduced metabolic rates compared to other insectivorous birds of equivalent mass. The 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C] body temperature at which these metabolic measurements were taken is typical for caprimulgids during their nocturnal active period. Interestingly, the lifetime reproductive success of individuals, given the single-egg annual clutch strategy, is heavily dependent on achieving this substantial longevity, as even a modest reduction in the number of breeding seasons can have profound consequences for the per-capita contribution to the next generation.
